name: Krishna Temple, Rawalpindi
significance: Rawalpindi's principal working Hindu temple, raised in 1897 in the Saddar quarter by two local businessmen, the brothers Kanji Mal and Ujagar Mal Ram Rachpal. Shut during the Partition violence and reopened in 1949, it now serves some 7,000 Hindus of Rawalpindi and Islamabad and has been restored with Punjab government funding since 2018.

name: Kalat Kali Temple
significance: A Kali temple in the Shahi Bazaar of Kalat, ascribed to the pre-Islamic Sewa dynasty, from which the town's older names Kalat-i-Seba and Kalat-i-Nichari derive. Its marble image of the goddess standing on Shiva is reckoned the second largest Kali statue in Asia; looted and broken in 1909-10, it was mended and reconsecrated, and a three-day festival is kept each January.

name: Umarkot Shiv Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple in Umerkot whose lingam is the focus of a three-day Maha Shivaratri fair drawing around 250,000 pilgrims from across Sindh, among the largest religious gatherings in Pakistan. The present building was put up roughly a century ago by a local Muslim, a shrine of Durga stands behind the main temple, and the site is managed by the Pakistan Hindu Panchayat.
story: Local tradition holds that the spot was discovered when a cowherd saw one of his cows pouring her milk over a lingam there.

name: Dargah Pir Ratan Nath Jee
deity: Shiva, at the seat of the Nath saint Sri Ratan Nath
significance: A Shaiva shrine in Jhanda Bazar honouring Sri Ratan Nath of the Nath sampradaya, reopened after some sixty years of closure and, with the Kalibari Mandir, one of the only Hindu temples in daily use in Peshawar. Its chief observance is Maha Shivaratri and it is looked after by the Pakistan Hindu Council; a government-posted guard was shot dead at the premises in January 2016.

name: Kargah Buddha
significance: A standing Buddha some fifty feet tall carved into a cliff in the Kargah nallah about six miles west of Gilgit, dated to the 7th century and brought to notice in 1938-39. A monastery and three stupas excavated nearby in 1931 yielded Sanskrit manuscripts, marking the valley as a centre of Buddhism from roughly the 3rd to the 11th century.
story: Local folklore holds that the figure is a man-eating giantess whom a holy man pinned to the rock face to stop her preying on the villagers.

name: Churrio Jabal Durga Mata Temple
significance: A Durga temple atop the multicoloured granite hill of Churrio near Nagarparkar in Tharparkar district, Sindh. Thousands of pilgrims come through the year and about 200,000 at Shivratri, when devotees immerse cremation ashes in its sacred water; the hill itself is being cut away by government-licensed granite quarrying with dynamite.
